property_summary: Only the contract owner can make the contract send out its entire balance via withdrawAll (so after calling withdrawAll, the caller's balance does not increase unless caller is owner).
Only the owner can successfully call withdrawAll, so non-owners' calls must revert.
If caller is not the contract owner then calling withdrawAll must revert.
For all non-owners, withdrawAll must revert on the original contract
For all non-owners, withdrawAll must revert on the original contract.

For any caller who is the owner and any positive deposit amount sent to the contract, calling withdrawAll sends the entire contract balance to the caller (owner) leaving the contract balance zero; the mutant that sends to a hardcoded non-owner address breaks this by leaving the contract balance non-zero or sending funds to a non-owner.

For any caller who is the owner and any positive deposit amount, after the owner calls withdrawAll the contract's balance is zero (all held Ether is transferred to the owner); the mutant that sends the funds to a hardcoded non-owner breaks this by leaving the contract balance non-zero or making the owner not receive the funds.

For any address that is NOT the hardcoded burn address, when the owner calls withdrawAll after funding the contract, the contract's balance becomes zero (reference sends all balance to owner), but the mutant that always sends to the hardcoded dead address can leave the owner's balance unchanged while contract balance becomes zero — instead, we assert that the owner's balance increases by the contract balance before withdrawAll; the reference satisfies this for all admissible inputs (owner calling withdrawAll), the mutant breaks it for inputs where owner != burn address and nonzero balance.

For any owner caller and any positive funded balance, after the owner calls withdrawAll the owner's external balance increases by the contract's prior balance (i.e., owner receives all contract Ether); the mutant that sends funds to a hardcoded non-owner address breaks this by not increasing the owner's balance by that amount for some inputs.

For any owner caller and any funded contract balance, when the owner calls withdrawAll the owner's external balance increases by the contract's prior balance (the reference forwards all funds to msg.sender; the mutant sends to a hardcoded non-owner so this can fail for some inputs).

For any caller and any contract balance, calling withdrawAll forwards the call through C.withdraw so that a failing/contract revert in the recipient causes withdrawAll to revert (reference) whereas the mutant that does a direct transfer to msg.sender will not revert when the recipient's fallback reverts — so the rule: withdrawAll should propagate revert of the external call performed by withdraw; the mutant breaks this when the owner is a reverting contract.

For any owner address that is a contract which reverts when receiving funds, calling withdrawAll on the correct contract forwards the call to withdraw (which will attempt the external call and thus revert), so withdrawAll always reverts when the owner contract's receive/fallback reverts; the mutant that does a direct transfer to msg.sender can succeed or behave differently — therefore the reference always propagates a failing external transfer to a reverting owner contract while the mutant does not (so the property is violated for some fuzzed amounts/ether balances).

For any owner contract that reverts when sent Ether, calling withdrawAll on the correct C will always revert (propagating the failing external call), whereas the mutant that replaces the internal withdraw call with a direct transfer can behave differently and may not propagate the revert for some fuzzed balances.

For any owner contract that accepts or rejects Ether via a payable fallback/receive, C.withdrawAll always reverts when the owner’s fallback/receive reverts (it propagates the failing external transfer invoked through withdraw), but the mutant that replaces the internal withdraw call with a direct transfer can behave differently for some contract balances and owner behaviours, so there exist inputs (owner contract that reverts and a nonzero contract balance) where the reference reverts and the mutant does not.

For any owner contract that reverts when receiving Ether and any positive contract balance, calling withdrawAll on the reference C always reverts (propagates the failing external call) — the mutant that replaces the internal withdraw call with a direct transfer can succeed for some such inputs, breaking this rule.
Only the original owner can successfully withdraw the contract balance (calls to withdrawAll by non-owner must revert).
Only the contract owner can successfully call withdraw(uint) (calls by other addresses revert).
When run is invoked with caller == msg.sender, calling c.withdraw(amount) must not revert (i.e., reverted == false).
When caller == msg.sender, calling c.withdraw(amount) must not revert (i.e., reverted == false).

For any caller who is the owner and any withdrawal amount <= contract balance, calling withdraw transfers funds out of the contract in the reference implementation (so address(c).balance decreases by the withdrawn amount); the mutant that uses a low-level call and ignores the success can leave the contract balance unchanged if the external transfer fails (so the property is violated for some adversarial callee).

For any withdrawal amount and any callee address, when the owner calls withdraw the reference contract always reduces its balance by the requested amount (transfer reverts on failure), whereas the mutant using call and ignoring success may leave the contract balance unchanged if the callee intentionally fails; the test asserts that after owner withdraw the contract balance decreased by the requested amount.

For any owner-triggered withdraw(amount) call, the reference contract always reduces its own balance by the requested amount (transfer either succeeds or reverts), while the mutant using call and ignoring the success can leave the contract balance unchanged when the recipient deliberately fails; the test fuzzes amount and uses a failing recipient helper to exhibit the difference.

For any owner-initiated withdraw(amount) call where the contract has sufficient balance, the reference contract always reduces address(c).balance by exactly amount (transfer reverts on failure), whereas the mutant that uses call and ignores the success may not reduce the contract balance when the recipient intentionally fails.
After sendMoney to a contract that consumes more than 2300 gas (via its fallback), depositsCount increments by 1 (i.e., call forwards enough gas to trigger the target's fallback effect).

property_summary: Calling sendMoney on any target with nonzero value never reverts when the caller is the owner and the target is an EOA (i.e., non-contract address).
If the target address has no code (is an EOA), then c.sendMoney(target, amount, "") must not revert when called by the owner.
If the target is an EOA (has no code), then calling c.sendMoney(target, amount, "") as c.owner must not revert.
If target is an EOA (address(target).code.length == 0), then calling c.sendMoney(target, amount, "") as the owner should not revert.

For any target that reverts when called with arbitrary calldata, the reference contract's low-level call (call) allows the callee's fallback/receive to execute arbitrary logic (including increasing C's depositsCount via reentrant or other side-effects), whereas replacing call with send (which only forwards 2300 gas) can make such callee executions fail; therefore the general rule: calling sendMoney on C that forwards enough gas (call) can trigger the callee's fallback and change depositsCount, while the buggy send-based variant will prevent that for some inputs (failing to forward sufficient gas).

For any target that executes payable fallback/receive logic when it is sent sufficient gas, C.sendMoney using call will allow that fallback to run (possibly increasing C.depositsCount via that external logic), whereas replacing call with send (2300 gas) can prevent the fallback from executing and thus leave depositsCount unchanged for some inputs.

For any target address with a payable fallback that increments C.depositsCount when invoked, the correct contract's sendMoney (using low-level call forwarding all gas) will allow that fallback to run and increment depositsCount for some payment amounts, whereas the mutant using send (2300 gas) can prevent the fallback from running and thus leave depositsCount unchanged for those inputs.

For any target contract whose payable fallback increments C.depositsCount, C.sendMoney(...) using a full low-level call will allow that fallback to run and thus can increase C.depositsCount for some payment amounts, whereas replacing call with send (which forwards only 2300 gas) can cause the fallback not to run and therefore C.depositsCount may remain unchanged for the same inputs.

For any target address, when sendMoney forwards full gas (using call) the target's payable fallback can execute and can change C.depositsCount; replacing call with send (2300 gas) can prevent the fallback from executing so there exist inputs (a payable, gas-consuming fallback) for which depositsCount observed after sendMoney differs between the correct and mutant contracts.
If a sendMoney call to a target address fails, the transaction must revert and leave the target not credited (i.e., a failed external call causes overall revert).
sendMoney must revert when the external call to _target fails (i.e., reverted == true whenever the forwarded call returns false).

property_summary: sendMoney always reverts (call completes with reverted==true) when the provided _target address has no payable fallback to accept the forwarded value.
Only the owner can cause ether to leave the contract via sendMoney (so non-owners cannot reduce the contract balance).
Only the owner can successfully call sendMoney — calls from non-owners always revert.
Calls to sendMoney from non-owner addresses always revert (i.e., only owner can successfully call sendMoney).
If sendMoney is invoked by an address that is not the contract owner, the call must revert (i.e., non-owners cannot successfully call sendMoney).
If sendMoney is called by an address that is not the contract owner, the call must revert and the contract balance must remain unchanged.

Only the owner can cause the contract to send Ether out: for every caller and input, calling sendMoney(...) on the correct contract does not decrease the contract balance unless the caller is the owner; the mutant removing the onlyOwner check allows a non-owner caller to make the contract send Ether and thus can decrease address(c).balance for some inputs.

For every caller and calldata, calls to sendMoney on the correct contract never decrease address(c).balance when the caller is non-owner (only the owner can make the contract send funds); the mutant removing the onlyOwner guard allows a non-owner caller to cause the contract balance to decrease for some inputs.

The reference contract increments depositsCount on every fallback payable call regardless of caller, while the mutant (which removes onlyOwner) allows non-owner to invoke sendMoney to make an external call that can revert and thus prevent depositsCount from reflecting expected behaviour—so a general rule: calling sendMoney from any caller never changes depositsCount, but onlyOwner removal can cause observable differences after a failing external call invoked by sendMoney (some inputs produce differing depositsCount).

For every caller and calldata, calling sendMoney(...) on the correct contract never causes the contract to forward Ether (i.e., address(c).balance does not decrease) unless the caller is the owner; the mutant removes the onlyOwner guard so a non-owner caller can cause the contract balance to drop for some inputs.
